screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we focus on two complementary skills every Ethereum developer needs: reliably sending transactions that change contract state, and listening for contract events so your frontend stays in sync with on-chain activity. We then introduce smart contract events, why they are inexpensive to emit, and how they let a DApp update in real time without aggressive polling. screens.title: Calls versus Transactions
screens.narratorSegment: A single contract exposes two interaction modes: read-only calls and state-changing transactions. Read-only functions marked view or pure return data immediately and cost no gas. They are executed locally by your provider and do not create a transaction or change chain state. By contrast, when you change state you create a transaction that must be signed and broadcast, consuming gas and waiting to be mined. This distinction matters for UX and cost: use calls for quick data checks and transactions when you intend to update on-chain state. A common misconception is treating a returned TransactionResponse as confirmation. The TransactionResponse simply confirms the transaction has been broadcast; it does not guarantee the EVM executed your change successfully. You must wait for a TransactionReceipt to verify status. A practical example: checking a token balance uses a call, but transferring tokens requires a transaction signed by the user. When designing flows, show immediate read-only data instantly and clearly indicate pending state for transactions until you verify the receipt. How will your UI differentiate these two user expectations? Calls versus Transactions means calls are gas-free reads; transactions are signed, gas-consuming operations that must be confirmed to ensure success.. In practical terms, when to read state and when to change it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Calls vs Transactions
Concept
Calls (view/pure) return values locally without gas. Transactions require a signer, spend gas, and change state once mined.
Example: getBalance() is a call. transfer(to, amount) is a transaction and requires wallet approval.
Misconception: Receiving a transaction hash equals success. Always wait for the receipt to confirm execution.
Visual Comparison
Call
No gas, immediate, no receipt, good for UI reads.
Transaction
Requires signer, gas cost, broadcast -> mined -> receipt.
Key Takeaway

Design your UI to show immediate reads for calls and a clear pending flow for transactions until the receipt confirms success.

screens.title: Transaction Lifecycle
screens.narratorSegment: The transaction lifecycle describes the stages a state-changing operation goes through on the network. When a user signs and sends a transaction it is first broadcast to the p2p network. Nodes include it in their mempool and it sits in pending state until a validator includes it in a mined block. After mining you receive a TransactionReceipt. At this point you often wait for additional block confirmations to reduce the small risk of a chain reorganization. Practically, Ethers. js returns a TransactionResponse once the transaction is broadcast. That object has a hash and other metadata, but not execution status. Calling tx. wait() pauses your flow until the block is mined and returns the TransactionReceipt which contains the status (1 for success, 0 for revert), gasUsed, emitted events, and blockNumber. A concrete example: show a spinner after broadcast, call tx. wait(), and then check receipt. status. If unsuccessful, surface the revert to the user and provide guidance. This pattern prevents premature success messages and keeps users correctly informed about on-chain outcomes. Transaction Lifecycle means broadcast -> pending -> mined -> confirmed. transactionresponse ≠ confirmed; use tx.wait() to obtain the transactionreceipt.. In practical terms, broadcast, pending, mined, and confirmed. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Lifecycle steps
keyIdea.text: Broadcast -> Pending -> Mined -> Confirmed. TransactionResponse ≠ confirmed; use tx.wait() to obtain the TransactionReceipt.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Transaction Lifecycle
Stages
  1. Broadcast: User signs and sends, TransactionResponse returned.
  2. Pending: Transaction propagates in the mempool until mined.
  3. Mined: Included in a block; tx.wait() returns a receipt for 1 confirmation by default.
  4. Confirmed: Optionally wait for more confirmations to reduce reorg risk.
Example: After sending a setLastMessage transaction, set UI to 'pending', call tx.wait(), then show success only if receipt.status === 1.
Receipt contents
  • status: 1 success, 0 revert.
  • gasUsed: gas consumed by execution.
  • blockNumber: block where tx was mined.
  • events: logs emitted by the contract during execution.
Misconception

Treating broadcast as final leads to false 'success' messages. Always inspect the receipt for execution status.

screens.title: Contract Instances & Signers
screens.narratorSegment: To send transactions you must use a Contract instance that has a Signer. A provider alone allows you to call view functions. A signer proves the user authorized the action and can sign the transaction payload, enabling gas payment. In Ethers. js you typically create a contract like new ethers. Contract(address, abi, signerOrProvider). When you pass a signer, methods that change state will prompt the wallet to sign. A common pattern is to prefer the wallet's signer for transactions and the provider for reads. This separation avoids accidental transaction prompts during simple data reads. A concrete example: your DApp creates a contract with the connected wallet's signer when the user intends to interact. If the contract instance lacks a signer, attempting to call a state-changing function will fail; the code should check contract. signer and guide the user to connect their wallet. Consider also that signing is asynchronous and the UI should reflect the awaiting signature and later, the broadcast and confirmation states. This practice reduces unexpected rejections and clarifies user intent. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Send-and-wait
keyIdea.text: Send the transaction, await tx.wait(), then inspect receipt.status and events to confirm execution and update UI.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Send & Wait Example
Example code
async function sendDataTransaction(contract, newValue) {
  if (!contract.signer) {
    console.error("Contract instance must have a signer for transactions.");
    return;
  }
  try {
    const tx = await contract.set(newValue);
    console.log("Transaction sent. Hash:", tx.hash);
    const receipt = await tx.wait();
    if (receipt && receipt.status === 1) {
      alert(`Data set to ${newValue} in transaction ${tx.hash}`);
      return true;
    } else {
      alert(`Transaction ${tx.hash} failed or reverted.`);
      return false;
    }
  } catch (error) {
    console.error("Error sending transaction:", error);
    if (error.code === 4001) {
      alert("Transaction rejected by user.");
    } else {
      alert(`Transaction failed: ${error.message}`);
    }
    return false;
  }
}
Explanation
  • Check contract.signer to ensure transactions can be signed.
  • contract.set(...) returns a TransactionResponse with a hash once broadcast.
  • tx.wait() returns a TransactionReceipt containing status, gasUsed, and events.
  • Catch both broadcast errors (e.g., user rejected) and execution failures reported in the receipt.
Key Takeaway

Design UI to await the receipt before declaring success and handle error codes like 4001 separately.

Developers often inspect tx. hash to show a link in the UI, but they must not treat that hash as proof of success. The TransactionReceipt arrives after mining and contains the execution outcome. It has the status field, gasUsed, blockNumber, and an array of events emitted during execution. Use receipt. status === 1 to confirm success and handle status === 0 as a revert. A concrete example: after sending, set UI to 'Transaction pending: hash...'. Call tx. wait() to get the receipt. If the receipt shows status 0, surface the revert and optionally decode revert reasons on the backend; but at minimum do not claim success. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Response vs Receipt
TransactionResponse
Returned immediately after broadcast. Contains tx.hash and metadata but no execution status. Use it to show a pending link or hash to the user.
TransactionReceipt
Returned by tx.wait() after mining. Contains status, gasUsed, blockNumber, and events. Use receipt.status to confirm success.
Practical tip

Show a 'pending' state after the TransactionResponse and only show 'confirmed' after receipt.status === 1. This avoids false positives and keeps user expectations accurate.

screens.title: Gas Estimation
screens.narratorSegment: Gas estimation predicts how much gas a transaction will consume. Wallets and libraries perform a simulation to estimate gas before broadcasting so users are not surprised by failures. In Ethers. js you can call contract. myFunction. estimateGas(args) to get a gasLimit. If estimation fails it usually means the transaction would revert under current state or input values. This is a useful early signal to prevent wasted gas or unnecessary prompts. In practice, rely on the wallet's default estimation for most actions but use manual estimation when you need tighter control, for example to set a custom gas buffer. If estimateGas throws, surface a clear error and avoid broadcasting. A frequent mistake is to ignore estimation errors and attempt to send anyway, which leads to failed transactions and unhappy users. Also show a clear UI explanation when a revert is likely, e. g., 'This action will revert with the current inputs.' That keeps users informed and reduces failed transaction attempts. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Gas Estimation
How it works
estimateGas runs a simulated execution to calculate gas usage. Use it to detect likely reverts before spending gas. Wallets perform their own estimation too.
Example: const gasLimit = await contract.myFunction.estimateGas(arg1, arg2); If it throws, warn the user and do not send.
Best practices
  • Rely on wallet estimation for typical flows.
  • Use manual estimate when setting custom gas buffers.
  • Surface clear errors when estimation fails; do not broadcast blindly.

screens.title: Smart Contract Events
screens.narratorSegment: Smart contract events let contracts emit structured logs during execution. Events are inexpensive compared to storing data in storage slots and they appear in the TransactionReceipt as log entries. DApps can listen to those events in real time to update UI, trigger notifications, or cache relevant data. screens.title: Subscribing to Events with Ethers.js
screens.narratorSegment: Ethers. js makes subscribing to events straightforward. You can attach a listener to a contract instance using contract. on(eventName, handler). The handler receives the event parameters and a final event object that contains metadata such as transactionHash. Listening this way provides real-time notifications so your UI can append new data without a refresh. The source code shows subscribing to ItemCreated and ItemSold and logging parameters. Remember to use indexed parameters in event declarations to make filtering efficient when you need targeted listeners. A concrete example: listening for ItemCreated, extract the itemId and owner from the event and prepend it to your UI list. Also plan for cleanup: if your component unmounts or the contract instance changes, remove the listener or call contract. removeAllListeners(). Forgetting to remove listeners causes duplicate handlers and memory leaks. Always pass the exact handler function so you can off() it correctly, or use a scoped removeAllListeners when appropriate. This keeps your app predictable and efficient. Handler considerations

Attaching multiple handlers for the same event when a component re-renders leads to duplicated UI updates. Remove handlers explicitly.

screens.title: Reliability Patterns and Common Challenges
screens.narratorSegment: Building a reliable transaction and event system requires handling a small set of real-world issues. Reorganizations can cause a recently mined transaction to be orphaned; to mitigate this, wait for more confirmations for critical flows by calling tx. wait(5) or a similarly higher confirmation count. Listener cleanup is essential: remove event listeners on component unmount or when the contract instance changes to prevent memory leaks and duplicate handlers. Use contract. removeAllListeners() when appropriate and prefer off(handler) with the same handler reference for precise cleanup. For error handling, distinguish between broadcast errors — such as user rejection or insufficient funds — and execution errors discovered after mining. Broadcast errors should be surfaced immediately and handled in catch blocks; execution errors are revealed by receipt. status === 0. Provide informative UI states: awaiting signature, broadcasting, pending confirmation, confirmed, or failed. Finally, surface gas estimation failures rather than attempting to send, and consider centralized indexers for complex queries. These practices make your DApp predictable and trustworthy for users. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we focus on two complementary skills every Ethereum developer needs: reliably sending transactions that change contract state, and listening for contract events so your frontend stays in sync with on-chain activity. You will learn the transaction lifecycle: from creating a transaction and broadcasting it, to waiting for it to be mined and checking the receipt for success or failure. We then introduce smart contract events, why they are inexpensive to emit, and how they let a DApp update in real time without aggressive polling. We'll show practical Ethers. js patterns: instantiating a Contract with a Signer, sending a transaction, using tx. wait() to obtain a TransactionReceipt, estimating gas, and subscribing to events with contract. on() or filtered listeners. Along the way we highlight common pitfalls: treating broadcast as confirmation, forgetting to remove listeners, and how reorganizations affect high-value flows. By the end you'll be able to implement a send-and-listen flow that updates the UI only after confirmation and reacts instantly when an event is emitted. Consider why events reduce load and improve UX: they let you react to the exact data the contract logged rather than re-fetching whole state. How will you show transaction progress to your users?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to distinguish between reading contract state and submitting transactions that change state. You will construct a Contract instance with a signer and submit a transaction, then use tx. wait() to obtain a TransactionReceipt and verify success. You will learn how gas estimation is used to predict cost and how to react when estimation fails. You will also understand Solidity events, why they are useful for DApps, and how to subscribe to them in Ethers. js. Each objective pairs a practical action with why it matters. For instance, waiting for a receipt prevents showing a premature success message; subscribing to events avoids expensive polling and keeps the UI responsive. Finally, you'll learn several reliability practices such as listener cleanup and considering extra confirmations for reorg protection. These skills let you build DApps that give users clear, accurate feedback and update in near real time.

This second objectives slide focuses on concrete developer actions and checks. You will practice estimating gas manually and understand when a failed estimation indicates a contract revert. You will implement event subscription patterns using contract. on() and filters built with contract. filters, and you'll learn why removing listeners matters to avoid memory leaks. We also cover distinguishing broadcast errors, such as a user rejection, from execution errors discovered after mining by checking receipt. status. Finally, you will learn to choose between live event listening and centralized indexers for heavy queries. For example, listening to a Minted event and adding the new token to the UI is efficient for near real-time updates, but an indexer is better for complex historical queries. These practical skills reduce user confusion and make production DApps more resilient.

A single contract exposes two interaction modes: read-only calls and state-changing transactions. Read-only functions marked view or pure return data immediately and cost no gas. They are executed locally by your provider and do not create a transaction or change chain state. By contrast, when you change state you create a transaction that must be signed and broadcast, consuming gas and waiting to be mined. This distinction matters for UX and cost: use calls for quick data checks and transactions when you intend to update on-chain state. A common misconception is treating a returned TransactionResponse as confirmation. The TransactionResponse simply confirms the transaction has been broadcast; it does not guarantee the EVM executed your change successfully. You must wait for a TransactionReceipt to verify status. A practical example: checking a token balance uses a call, but transferring tokens requires a transaction signed by the user. When designing flows, show immediate read-only data instantly and clearly indicate pending state for transactions until you verify the receipt. How will your UI differentiate these two user expectations? Calls versus Transactions means calls are gas-free reads; transactions are signed, gas-consuming operations that must be confirmed to ensure success.. In practical terms, when to read state and when to change it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The transaction lifecycle describes the stages a state-changing operation goes through on the network. When a user signs and sends a transaction it is first broadcast to the p2p network. Nodes include it in their mempool and it sits in pending state until a validator includes it in a mined block. After mining you receive a TransactionReceipt. At this point you often wait for additional block confirmations to reduce the small risk of a chain reorganization. Practically, Ethers. js returns a TransactionResponse once the transaction is broadcast. That object has a hash and other metadata, but not execution status. Calling tx. wait() pauses your flow until the block is mined and returns the TransactionReceipt which contains the status (1 for success, 0 for revert), gasUsed, emitted events, and blockNumber. A concrete example: show a spinner after broadcast, call tx. wait(), and then check receipt. status. If unsuccessful, surface the revert to the user and provide guidance. This pattern prevents premature success messages and keeps users correctly informed about on-chain outcomes. Transaction Lifecycle means broadcast -> pending -> mined -> confirmed. transactionresponse ≠ confirmed; use tx.wait() to obtain the transactionreceipt.. In practical terms, broadcast, pending, mined, and confirmed. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

To send transactions you must use a Contract instance that has a Signer. A provider alone allows you to call view functions. A signer proves the user authorized the action and can sign the transaction payload, enabling gas payment. In Ethers. js you typically create a contract like new ethers. Contract(address, abi, signerOrProvider). When you pass a signer, methods that change state will prompt the wallet to sign. A common pattern is to prefer the wallet's signer for transactions and the provider for reads. This separation avoids accidental transaction prompts during simple data reads. A concrete example: your DApp creates a contract with the connected wallet's signer when the user intends to interact. If the contract instance lacks a signer, attempting to call a state-changing function will fail; the code should check contract. signer and guide the user to connect their wallet. Consider also that signing is asynchronous and the UI should reflect the awaiting signature and later, the broadcast and confirmation states. This practice reduces unexpected rejections and clarifies user intent. Contract Instances & Signers means a signer is required to authorize state changes. use provider for reads and a signer-attached contract for transactions.. In practical terms, why a signer is required for transactions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through a practical send-and-wait pattern. The typical steps are: ensure the contract instance has a signer, call the state-changing method which returns a TransactionResponse, and then call tx. wait() to get the TransactionReceipt. In the provided example function, the contract. set(newValue) call returns immediately with tx, then tx. wait() pauses the code until the block includes the transaction. The receipt tells you if the transaction executed successfully and what events were emitted. A concrete example: setting a numeric value in a simple storage contract. We show how to alert the user on success and handle errors such as user rejection or revert. A common pitfall is handling errors only at the broadcast step. You must also check receipt. status === 1 after waiting, because a transaction may be mined but still revert. When designing UI flows, show 'waiting for confirmation' after broadcast and only show final success when the receipt confirms execution. Now review the code block to see how logging, try/catch, and user alerts are arranged to provide clear feedback. Sending a Transaction and Waiting means send the transaction, await tx.wait(), then inspect receipt.status and events to confirm execution and update ui.. Ethers. js provides two related but distinct objects when you send a transaction. The TransactionResponse is returned immediately after broadcast. It includes the transaction hash, chain id, and some metadata, but not execution status. Developers often inspect tx. hash to show a link in the UI, but they must not treat that hash as proof of success. The TransactionReceipt arrives after mining and contains the execution outcome. It has the status field, gasUsed, blockNumber, and an array of events emitted during execution. Use receipt. status === 1 to confirm success and handle status === 0 as a revert. A concrete example: after sending, set UI to 'Transaction pending: hash...'. Call tx. wait() to get the receipt. If the receipt shows status 0, surface the revert and optionally decode revert reasons on the backend; but at minimum do not claim success. This clear distinction prevents situations where users see a success message for a transaction that later reverts, which damages trust in your DApp. TransactionResponse vs TransactionReceipt means transactionresponse indicates broadcast; transactionreceipt confirms execution. always check receipt.status for finality.. Gas estimation predicts how much gas a transaction will consume. Wallets and libraries perform a simulation to estimate gas before broadcasting so users are not surprised by failures. In Ethers. js you can call contract. myFunction. estimateGas(args) to get a gasLimit. If estimation fails it usually means the transaction would revert under current state or input values. This is a useful early signal to prevent wasted gas or unnecessary prompts. In practice, rely on the wallet's default estimation for most actions but use manual estimation when you need tighter control, for example to set a custom gas buffer. If estimateGas throws, surface a clear error and avoid broadcasting. A frequent mistake is to ignore estimation errors and attempt to send anyway, which leads to failed transactions and unhappy users. Also show a clear UI explanation when a revert is likely, e. g., 'This action will revert with the current inputs.' That keeps users informed and reduces failed transaction attempts. Smart contract events let contracts emit structured logs during execution. Events are inexpensive compared to storing data in storage slots and they appear in the TransactionReceipt as log entries. DApps can listen to those events in real time to update UI, trigger notifications, or cache relevant data. For example, an ERC721 contract emits a Transfer event on token transfer; the frontend can listen to that event and add the token to a user's collection without polling for balances. Events are the primary mechanism for reactive frontends interacting with on-chain activity. In your contract you declare event signatures and emit them at important points. For example, an ItemCreated event might include an itemId and owner. When building UIs, rely on events for incremental updates and use historical queries for complete reconstructions. A common misconception is that events alone replace on-chain state; they should augment state reads. Events provide fast notifications but you should verify critical state by reading contract storage when needed. Solidity allows marking event parameters as indexed; Ethers. js exposes contract. filters to create precise filters based on those indexed fields. When you care about events involving a specific address or id, filters dramatically reduce data volume. Building a reliable transaction and event system requires handling a small set of real-world issues. Reorganizations can cause a recently mined transaction to be orphaned; to mitigate this, wait for more confirmations for critical flows by calling tx. wait(5) or a similarly higher confirmation count. Listener cleanup is essential: remove event listeners on component unmount or when the contract instance changes to prevent memory leaks and duplicate handlers. Use contract. removeAllListeners() when appropriate and prefer off(handler) with the same handler reference for precise cleanup. For error handling, distinguish between broadcast errors — such as user rejection or insufficient funds — and execution errors discovered after mining. Broadcast errors should be surfaced immediately and handled in catch blocks; execution errors are revealed by receipt. status === 0. Provide informative UI states: awaiting signature, broadcasting, pending confirmation, confirmed, or failed. Finally, surface gas estimation failures rather than attempting to send, and consider centralized indexers for complex queries. These practices make your DApp predictable and trustworthy for users. Let's summarize the most important ideas. First, the transaction lifecycle: a transaction is broadcast, becomes pending, may be mined into a block, and then confirmed. Use tx. wait() to obtain the receipt and check receipt. status. Second, events are logs emitted by contracts that frontends can subscribe to with contract. on(); they are cheap and ideal for incremental updates. Third, always attach a signer to a Contract instance when you intend to send transactions, and perform gas estimation where helpful. Finally, practice listener hygiene by removing handlers when no longer needed and consider extra confirmations for high-value operations. These practices deliver a reliable, real-time user experience while avoiding common pitfalls such as false success messages and memory leaks.
